solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Explosive rhythm section better

blocks.note: the drums and other percussion instruments form a band's rhythm section
to cap something is to better or outdo it

explanation.surface: A music critic raves that a band's drummers and bassist are better than explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosive' reads as praise for the band, but it is a noun here; 'better' is a verb, not a comparison.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussion cap is a small charge that detonates when struck, used to fire old guns and toy pistols, so it is an explosive.

clue.text: Introductions having PA accepting job — good sign

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece receives the others inside it

blocks.note: taken as written; it will be split around the middle
a job is a role
G is the standard abbreviation for good
an omen is a sign of things to come

explanation.surface: A personal assistant takes on a new job and treats the introductions as a good omen.
explanation.walkthrough: PA opens up to hold ROLE, G and OMEN in a row: P + ROLEGOMEN + A.
explanation.definitionFit: Prolegomena are formal prefatory remarks or essays opening a scholarly book, a learned plural word for preliminary introductions.

clue.text: Star‘s gear held without case

indicators.note: a case is the outer covering, so taking it away leaves only the interior letters

blocks.note: rig is equipment or gear
the inner letters of the word, with first and last dropped

explanation.surface: A celebrity's kit is being kept loose, not packed in a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star's' is the definition plus 's for 'is'; the star is not a celebrity but a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigel is the bright blue-white supergiant forming the foot of the constellation Orion, one of the brightest stars in the night sky.

clue.text: Breaking up fun, he’ll become awkward

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe and comma ignored

explanation.surface: A spoilsport who breaks up the fun will soon be seen as awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking up' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'up' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone awkward is obstructive and uncooperative, refusing to make things easy, which is what being unhelpful means.

clue.text: Dog Zeus initially confined to his hut that’s barking

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted
something confined is shut inside, so one piece sits within the other
barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the first letter of the god's name
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A god's dog is kept in its kennel, barking away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' suits a dog in the surface, but in British slang it means crazy, signalling the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The shih tzu is a small long-haired toy breed of dog originally from Tibet and China.

clue.text: Concealed missing can-opener? Open!

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so these letters are taken away

blocks.note: covert means hidden or concealed
the opening letter of 'can', the piece removed

explanation.surface: Someone hunting for a hidden tin-opener gives up and cries 'Open!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can-opener' is the first letter of 'can', not a kitchen tool; dropping it from the word for concealed leaves its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means done openly and plainly visible, not hidden, so it matches open as an adjective.

clue.text: Vehicle needs wire, initially tense for crossing Spanish river

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so only the first letter is used
a bridge crossing a gap spans it, so one piece stretches over and around the other

blocks.note: a cable is a wire
the opening letter of the word
río is Spanish for river

explanation.surface: A car needs its wiring fixed before tensely crossing a river in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spanish river' tempts a solver to recall a named river such as the Ebro, but it is simply the Spanish word for river.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabriolet is a convertible car with a folding roof, or originally a light horse-drawn carriage, so it is a vehicle.

clue.text: Piece trimmed becomes level

indicators.note: trimming cuts off the end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: a part is a piece of something

explanation.surface: A carpenter trims a piece of wood until it lies level.
explanation.walkthrough: PART loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Par means an equal standing, as in 'on a par', so it is a level of equality.

clue.text: Water pipe new that comes into Slough

indicators.note: coming into a place means entering it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a slough is a swamp or bog; Slough is also an English town, the surface reading
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A new water main is being laid into the town of Slough, west of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire town, capitalised for the surface, but it is the common noun for a swamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A bong is a pipe that draws smoke through water to cool it, typically used for smoking cannabis.

clue.text: Scientist here’s being strange

indicators.note: strange means odd or abnormal, so the letters are put into an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A boffin remarks that existence is a strange business.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the physicist famous for uncertainty is clued by a strange being.
explanation.definitionFit: Werner Heisenberg was the German physicist who founded quantum mechanics and formulated the uncertainty principle.

clue.text: Moorland accommodation bombed

blocks.note: a fell is upland moor in northern England
a flat is an apartment, a place to live

explanation.surface: A lodge out on the moors was hit in an air raid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombed' suggests an air raid, but it is the informal sense of a show or joke failing.
explanation.definitionFit: To bomb is to fail utterly, and a joke or performance that fell flat got no response from its audience.

clue.text: Fish on time to keep an eye on birds?

definitions.note: the question mark flags the hobbyist's slang sense

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another follows it, setting the order of the parts

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
the witch is a flatfish related to the flounder

explanation.surface: A cat sits by the fish tank, timing its moment while eyeing the birds outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The witch, or witch flounder, is an obscure flatfish known mainly to crossword setters.
explanation.definitionFit: Twitching is British slang for keen birdwatching, especially travelling to spot rare species, so to twitch is to watch birds.

clue.text: Gut pain with bad hooch quaffed by sons: they go from bar to bar!

definitions.text: they go from bar to bar!

indicators.note: bad means spoilt or corrupted, so the letters lose their proper order
a drink quaffed goes down inside the drinker, so one piece is swallowed by another

blocks.note: colic is a sharp abdominal pain
the five letters reordered
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Bootleg liquor gives some lads a stomach ache as they go on a pub crawl.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests drinkers moving between pubs; the bars are actually bars of chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocoholics are people addicted to chocolate, who would happily eat one chocolate bar after another.

clue.text: Hand in evidence Queen has left throne?

blocks.note: first meaning: the best possible poker hand, ace to ten of one suit
second meaning, playful: 'throne' is slang for a toilet, and a monarch rising leaves the sound of a regal cistern

explanation.surface: Proof that the monarch has abdicated, offered as a winning hand in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throne' is jokey slang for a toilet, so the queen's departure is announced by a flush; the question mark admits the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the top hand is ace, king, queen, jack and ten of one suit; and a flush is what is heard after the toilet is used.

clue.text: Shock when ducks upset horse

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, and in a down clue that turns the letters upside down

blocks.note: to appal is to shock
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, and an O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A horse gets a fright when some ducks are knocked over beside it.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a score of zero, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: The Appaloosa is a North American breed of horse with a distinctive spotted coat, developed by the Nez Perce people.

clue.text: Hard work put an end to childish game

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
op is short for opus, a work
to scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it

explanation.surface: A strict parent ends the children's play by setting them hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: OP is short for opus, a musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is a playground game in which children hop through numbered squares chalked on the ground, so it is a game for kids.

clue.text: … King on it makes appearance!

indicators.note: in an across clue one part sitting on another comes after it, which fixes the order

blocks.note: the ellipsis carries on from 13 across, where 'it' was the throne, slang for a toilet; loo is British for toilet
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Continuing the royal joke from 13 across, a king appears seated on the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie this to 13 across: 'it' is the throne there, a toilet, and the loo is the everyday British word for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A look is someone's appearance or style, as in 'a new look', so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Joe leaps on and off vehicle GIs use?

indicators.note: on and off means intermittently, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: An American soldier, a GI Joe, hops in and out of the army runabout.
explanation.walkthrough: GI Joe is a nickname for a US soldier, so Joe leaping on and off suits the surface perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: The jeep is the small rugged four-wheel-drive vehicle used by American troops since the Second World War.

clue.text: Nothing at court helping Romeo out — here’s philtre

indicators.note: out means gone or excluded, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: in tennis a score of nil is love
a helping of food is a portion
R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Juliet's Romeo is nowhere at court, so someone offers a magic drink to help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' is a tennis court, not a royal one; Romeo is the radio code word for R, not Shakespeare's lover.
explanation.definitionFit: A philtre is a magic drink meant to make the drinker fall in love, which is exactly what a love potion is.

clue.text: One in burning heap we hear after five in the morning?

definitions.text: One in burning heap we hear after five in the morning?

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling follows the pronunciation

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
a.m. marks the morning hours
a pyre is a heap set alight; 'One in' tells us to spell it with I, the one

explanation.surface: Someone is caught on a bonfire at dawn, at five in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a vampire caught by sunrise bursts into flame, becoming a burning heap.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend sunlight destroys these undead bloodsuckers, so after dawn any of them left outside would be reduced to ashes.

clue.text: Bitterness amiss in American pollster

blocks.note: gall is bitterness or rancour
when something is amiss we ask 'what's up?'

explanation.surface: An American opinion pollster is sour because his figures went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amiss' looks like an anagram signal, but it gives UP, as in 'something is up'.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gallup was the American who pioneered scientific opinion polling, and his company's Gallup poll still bears his name.

clue.text: Gypsy man features in Post Office advertisement

indicators.note: to feature in something is to appear within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: PO is the abbreviation for Post Office
a Rom is a Romani man

explanation.surface: A Romani man appears in an advert for the Post Office.
explanation.walkthrough: ROM is the Romani people's own word for a man of their community.
explanation.definitionFit: A promo is informal for a promotional item, such as a short film or flyer advertising a product.

clue.text: Who’s Keith to keep a jam jar for biscuit?

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: Keith Moon was the drummer of The Who
taken as written
jam jar is Cockney rhyming slang for car

explanation.surface: Someone asks who Keith is, that he gets to keep a jam jar for biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who's' is not a question: Keith Moon drummed for the rock band The Who. Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a rhyming phrase, so jam jar means car.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaroon is a light biscuit made from ground almonds or coconut with egg white and sugar.

clue.text: No knight, evidently, taking queen in game

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it within, so one piece gets inserted

blocks.note: a roué is a debauched rake, plainly no chivalrous knight
Q is the chess abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: A chess player who has no knight left is taking the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess setting suggests pieces, but 'No knight' cryptically describes a rake who is anything but chivalrous.
explanation.definitionFit: Roque is an American variant of croquet played on a hard court with a raised border, so it is a lawn game.

clue.text: Returning black and white cab crosses street for class expert

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the letters run backwards
to cross something can be to straddle it, so one piece spans the other

blocks.note: monochrome, shortened to mono, is black and white
a cab is a taxi
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A black-and-white taxi turns back across the road carrying a teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black and white cab' looks like a description of a taxi's paint, but 'black and white' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxonomist classifies living things into ranks such as class, order and genus, so is an expert in biological classification.

clue.text: Wood turned this way? Odd bits discarded

indicators.note: throwing away the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even-placed ones
turned around means facing back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A woodturner shapes timber on the lathe and discards the odd offcuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' suits woodturning in the surface but signals reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is the pale tough timber of the ash tree, used for tool handles and furniture.

clue.text: Leave somewhat short

indicators.note: something short falls shy of its full length, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: quite means somewhat, as in quite good

explanation.walkthrough: The three words read like a phrase about leaving a bit early, but 'short' acts on the middle word.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit is to go away from a place or job, so it can replace leave as a verb.

clue.text: So in love with dominant rotter?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for being utterly smitten
second meaning, playful: a boss (a head) placed above scoundrels (heels), which is what the phrase literally describes

explanation.surface: Someone is besotted with a domineering cad.
explanation.walkthrough: A heel is an old word for a cad or rotter, and a head is a person in charge; the question mark flags the literal reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Being head over heels is the idiom for being completely and helplessly infatuated with somebody.
